papers.title: Short-horizon mean reversion in cryptocurrency markets: a matched cross-market measurement (Kitron & Wengrowicz)
papers.asset_and_horizon: 183 Binance USDT spot pairs (BTC included) vs 187 US stocks/ETFs; 15m primary, also 5m, 1h, 4h. Label is intra-bar open-to-close up/down, the same target as Polymarket's hourly market.
papers.method_and_features: 3-parameter kernel-constrained autoregressive logit on the last 12 soft-clipped bar returns (essentially betting against the previous bar's sign, weighted by size), plus an unconstrained AR(12) logit and a model-free sign correlation. Baselines include tuned gradient-boosted trees and an MLP on the same lags. Taker-flow imbalance and order-book depth used for conditioning.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Strict walk-forward: train 5,760 / test 960 candles, non-overlapping test blocks scored once (1h: 2,160/360). Primary window 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-11. Design fixed before the wide-universe run. Frozen 6-month holdout 2026-02-12 to 2026-08-08. Moving-block bootstrap, permutation null, shuffled-label and sign-randomization controls, one-bar feature/label gap, cross-venue refetches. Look-ahead risk low. Caveats: universe ranked on post-sample volume (an ex-ante subset is also reported), flat bars counted as 'down' inflate scores slightly, fit-conditional headline is optimistic by a third to a half.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: BTC 15m OOS (n=33,312): AUC 0.533 [0.527, 0.539], '52.3% unthresholded accuracy on BTC'. Accuracy rises to about 56% only on the most confident few percent of bars. Horizon decay (mean of focal crypto coins): AUC 0.536 at 15m, 0.521 at 1h, 0.496 at 4h. All 4 coins significant at 1h under the constrained logit. No BTC-only 1h AUC given. On btc-1h, OOS log-loss: constrained logit 0.6918 vs base rate 0.6931; free logit 0.6935, GBM 0.6933, MLP 0.7005, so trees and the MLP were worse than predicting the base rate. Holdout 2026-02 to 2026-08: crypto mean AUC 0.522 at 15m, down from 0.531.
papers.costs_considered: Yes. Gross edge per trade peaks near 1.3 bp (BTC/ETH 15m) against a 5 bp cheapest spot maker round trip and 10-20 bp taker. No pair out of 183 clears even the maker band at any threshold. 5m bars are worse (0.15 bp). Costs are in bps of notional, so they don't map directly to a binary payoff.
papers.credibility_reason: Best-designed study found: pre-fixed protocol, walk-forward, forward holdout on data that didn't exist at design time, permutation and sign-randomization nulls, artifact battery, honest effect sizes and cost pricing. Downsides: not peer-reviewed, authors disclose they run a trading system based on a variant of this model, and hourly results are only summarized for 4 coins.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Bitcoin Trading Under Transaction Costs: Evidence From Walk-Forward Forecasting (Bysik & Ślepaczuk)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Binance BTC/USDT USD-M perpetual futures, next-1-hour close-to-close log return, ~70,000 hourly bars 2018-2025.
papers.method_and_features: XGBoost, LSTM, iTransformer on three nested feature sets: OHLCV; OHLCV plus 10 technical indicators selected per fold (from 94 candidates, windows 3-336h, via block-wise Spearman ranking on train only); plus EGARCH volatility features. Sign rule (long-only or long-short), plus a cost-aware filter that trades only when |forecast| > λ·cost.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Rolling non-anchored walk-forward: 12-month train, 3-month validation, 3-month test, stepped 3 months, giving 27 test folds covering 2018-2025. Features, scaling and indicators computed causally inside each fold. Paired circular block bootstrap (24/72/168h blocks) with Holm correction. Look-ahead risk low. Many configurations (3 models x 3 feature sets x 2 losses x 3 selectors x 2 modes x λ grid) raise selection risk.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Not reported numerically in the sections read. The text only calls the flagship's hit rate 'positive but moderate'. Trading OOS 2018-2025: naive long-only XGBoost gross annualized return 73.50% vs buy-and-hold 56.35%. At 10 bp per position change it becomes −64.00% (10,619 trades); LSTM −50.65%, iTransformer −83.93%, 24h momentum −45.93%. Naive long-short XGBoost at 10 bp: −92.58%. Cost-aware long-only XGBoost: 65.40% annualized, Sharpe 1.09, 251 trades. Its Sharpe edge over buy-and-hold is not significant after bootstrap. 16 of 27 folds profitable, median fold return 7.98%.
papers.costs_considered: Yes: 10 bp per unit turnover (sensitivity 0-25 bp), built into the trading rule. No order-book depth, partial fills or maker/taker routing.
papers.credibility_reason: Proper walk-forward with costs, bootstrap inference, a buy-and-hold benchmark, and candid limits. The credible finding is the negative one: hourly sign-trading from ML forecasts fails after realistic costs. The positive filtered result is mostly long-BTC exposure, is not significantly better than buy-and-hold, and is sparse (median 4 trades per fold). No direction accuracy reported, which is a gap for this question.

papers.title: OpenMarket: A Synchronized Polymarket-Binance Dataset for High-Frequency Prediction-Market Research (Young)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Polymarket BTC 15-minute Up/Down binary markets vs Binance BTC/USDT order flow. Settlement of each 15-minute window.
papers.method_and_features: Walk-forward logistic regression with Platt scaling on 43 features: order-book spread, microprice, imbalance, depth, update velocity; returns, realized vol, momentum, VWAP deviation, candle shape; technical indicators. Baselines: Polymarket mid-price prior at the same timestamp, drift-only, order-flow imbalance only.
papers.out_of_sample_design: 559 walk-forward windows by market; model and calibrator fit only on pre-cutoff rows. 355,814 strictly OOS scored rows across 2,251 markets, event data 2026-02-12 to 2026-05-15 (54 observed days). The paper flags that full-timeline numbers include training rows and reports them only as diagnostics. Rows within one market are highly correlated, so the effective sample is closer to about 2,000 markets.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Accuracy not reported. Pooled walk-forward OOS: logistic AUC 0.8377, Brier 0.165, ECE 0.026 vs Polymarket mid prior AUC 0.8405, Brier 0.163, ECE 0.014, so the model slightly underperforms the market price. The high AUCs come from rows sampled inside live windows after price has moved; these are not window-open forecasts. Order-flow imbalance alone: AUC 0.5863 (diagnostic full timeline).
papers.costs_considered: Yes: simulated positive-EV trading at 1% fee plus 0.5% slippage nets −0.116 normalized payoff units per attempted trade. Top-of-book spread is usually 1 tick (median 0.01).
papers.credibility_reason: Directly relevant venue, honest walk-forward null with the right baseline (the market's own price, not 50%). Limits: only 54 days, single author, logistic model only (trees and sequence models listed as future work), fee model is a flat assumption rather than Polymarket's p(1−p) schedule, and it covers 15-minute rather than hourly markets.

papers.title: The Quarter-Hour Effect: Periodic Algorithmic Trading and Return Predictability in Cryptocurrency Futures (Kim & Hansen)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Binance USDT-M perpetuals (BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL, DOGE, ADA). The forecast target is the first 10-second return after each quarter-hour boundary; order imbalance at the boundary is also tested against 4-12h forward returns.
papers.method_and_features: Rolling LASSO and L1-logistic regression on 12 quarter-hour-spaced lags of the opening 10-second return plus 28 technical indicators on the 15-minute OHLCV grid. HAC regressions of forward returns on quarter-hour opening order imbalance.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Monthly refit on the trailing 6 months; penalty chosen on the chronological last 20% of each training window. OOS 2021-07-01 to 2024-10-31 (40 refits, ~117,000 boundaries per asset). Predictors fixed at least 15 minutes before the boundary. The 4-12h order-imbalance results are full-sample regressions, not OOS direction forecasts. Placebo phase-shift grids used.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: For the 10-second opening return only: BTC Lag+TI28 AUC 0.6035, accuracy 57.30% (hit rate 57.1% in Table A.3). Six-asset mean AUC 0.6011, accuracy 57.12%. On a mid-price-anchored subsample (2023-05-16 to 2024-03-30), BTC accuracy 58.65%. No accuracy reported for 15m or 1h bar direction. The top-of-hour increment is statistically insignificant at 4h.
papers.costs_considered: Discussed, not simulated. BTC gross edge 0.375 bp per boundary (six-asset mean ~0.5 bp), about one tenth of a 5 bp taker fee. The authors frame it as an execution input, not a standalone strategy.
papers.credibility_reason: Rigorous rolling OOS by an established econometrician, with Diebold-Mariano tests, calibration checks and placebos. Low relevance to hourly direction: it shows that 57% accuracy on a tiny 10-second target is economically worthless after fees. The longer-horizon order-imbalance evidence is in-sample.

papers.title: Short-term bitcoin market prediction via machine learning (Jaquart, Dann & Weinhardt, Journal of Finance and Data Science 7:45-66)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Bitcoin (Bloomberg minutely price), horizons 1, 5, 15 and 60 minutes, predictions made every minute.
papers.method_and_features: GRU, LSTM, feedforward net, logistic regression, XGBoost (max depth 1), random forest, and an ensemble. Features: minutely BTC returns over a 120-minute history plus a 1-week return; MSCI World, S&P 500, VIX, gold, oil and FX returns; blockchain transactions and mempool growth; Twitter volume and sentiment. Label = next m-minute return ≥ training-set median.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Single chronological split of 2019-03-11 to 2019-12-10 (weekends dropped): ~5 months train, ~1 month validation, ~3 months test. Standardization from the training set. Targets at the 60-minute horizon overlap heavily because predictions are made every minute, yet the binomial p-values (e.g. 2.28E-297) assume independence, so significance is grossly overstated. One regime, one short test window.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Test ~Sep-Dec 2019. 60-min: LSTM 56.01%, GBC 55.70%, GRU 55.67%, RF 55.64%, ensemble 55.76%, LR 53.86%, FNN 52.96%. 15-min: 51.96% (LR) to 53.79% (ensemble). 5-min: 51.79% to 52.93%. 1-min: 50.94% to 51.93%. The authors summarize: 'accuracies ranging from 50.9% to 56.0%'.
papers.costs_considered: Yes: 30 bp round trip. A long-short strategy on the 1% probability quantile made up to 116% over the 3-month test before costs (buy-and-hold −29.58%), but performance was negative for every model after costs.
papers.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed, chronological split, several model families and costs. But a single 3-month test in 2019, overlapping labels with independence-based significance tests, and an old market regime. The ~55-56% hourly figures are likely optimistic and have not been replicated on recent data.

papers.title: Informer In Algorithmic Investment Strategies on High Frequency Bitcoin Data (Stefaniuk & Ślepaczuk)
papers.asset_and_horizon: BTC/USDT 5m, 15m and 30m bars, 2019-08-21 to 2024-07-24; next-bar return forecasts turned into long/short positions.
papers.method_and_features: Informer transformer trained with RMSE, Quantile, or GMADL (a direction-aware loss). Features: OHLCV-derived returns and volatility, SMA/EMA ratios, MACD, RSI, Bollinger ratios, hour-of-day and weekday. Benchmarks: buy-and-hold, MACD and RSI strategies.
papers.out_of_sample_design: 6 walk-forward windows, each with train, validation and test. Model hyperparameters were randomly searched (30 of 1.17M combinations) on the first window only and reused. Strategy entry/exit thresholds searched exhaustively (4,096 combinations) on each validation set. No statistical tests against buy-and-hold. High selection risk from the large search.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Not reported. Trading over concatenated test windows: GMADL Informer 5m final value 9.747x (annualized 115.9%, 846 trades) vs buy-and-hold 1.441x (13.1%). RSI 30m 4.542x. RMSE Informer 30m 2.727x. Quantile Informer 30m 0.629x. Results vary greatly by window; e.g. GMADL 15m gained 382% annualized in one window and lost 48.9% in another.
papers.costs_considered: Yes, a 0.1% fee per position change. The paper notes RMSE forecasts at 5m/15m were mostly smaller than the fee.
papers.credibility_reason: Walk-forward with fees, but heavy threshold and hyperparameter search, tuning done on one window, no significance tests, no accuracy metric, and one winning configuration out of many. Results are consistent with selection luck.

papers.title: Kronos: A Foundation Model for the Language of Financial Markets (Shi et al., Tsinghua)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Pretrained on 12B+ K-line records from 45 exchanges. Evaluation includes all Binance spot pairs (OHLC only) pooled across 5m to daily frequencies (1h: 80-bar lookback, 12-bar horizon).
papers.method_and_features: Tokenized OHLCVA candles with a decoder-only autoregressive transformer, zero-shot. Compared with full-shot models (iTransformer, PatchTST, DLinear, etc.) and zero-shot TSFMs (TimesFM, Chronos, Moirai, Time-MoE).
papers.out_of_sample_design: Pretraining data through June 2024, tests from July 2024. Metrics are IC/RankIC pooled over all samples within an asset class and frequency, so they mix cross-sectional and time-series skill. The investment backtest covers only Chinese A-shares (daily, Qlib). No single-asset timing test.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Not reported. Crypto return forecasting IC: Kronos small/base/large 0.0373/0.0376/0.0368 (RankIC 0.0332/0.0336/0.0333), while full-shot DLinear scored higher IC at 0.0446. Crypto price-series RankIC: Kronos small 0.0138 vs PatchTST 0.0192. Kronos was not the best model on crypto in either table.
papers.costs_considered: Not for crypto. The A-share backtest uses top-k/drop-n with a 5-day minimum hold.
papers.credibility_reason: For this question: no direction accuracy, pooled IC not specific to BTC hourly, no crypto trading test, and weak crypto ICs where simple baselines match or beat it. Consistent with your 49-50% result. The paper's volatility-forecasting gains fit your finding that forecast spread predicts move size.

papers.title: Predictive Extrema, Unprofitable Policies: An AI-Assisted Audit of Candle-Based Binance Spot Timing Models (Jadouli)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Binance Spot BTC, ETH and SOL at 5m (local extrema, 30-120 min radius); a 10-pair 1-minute 4-hour target/stop selector; daily BTC/ETH extrema.
papers.method_and_features: 14 models (logistic, linear SVM, RF, histogram gradient boosting, MLP, CNN, GRU, LSTM, Transformer, hybrids) on 48 bars of OHLCV, indicators and clock features; ExtraTrees ranking for the 4h selector.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Train through 2026-03-31, validate April-June 2026 with label-horizon purging, evaluate July 1-12, 2026. The frozen selector ran July 1-19, 2026 unchanged, but after 946+ candidates were compared on April-June. Includes a forensic retraction of an earlier 'holdout' that had unpurged 4h labels, same-close entry and dates already exposed. Samples are tiny (9-19 cycles).
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: No next-bar up/down accuracy. Local-minimum detectors: ROC AUC up to 0.974 (HGB), but average precision 0.334 at 1.42% prevalence. Validation-selected model: 9 cycles, gross +11.1 bp, net −19.9 bp, −1.79%. Frozen 4h selector: 3 wins, 16 losses, −6.72% at 31 bp.
papers.costs_considered: Yes: 21/31/51 bp per completed cycle, next-open entry, adverse stop-first tie rule.
papers.credibility_reason: Candid negative audit with good hygiene (purging, next-open fills, provenance checks) and a useful red-flag catalogue. Evaluation samples are far too small to be conclusive either way, and it doesn't test the next-hour direction target directly.

papers.title: Forecasting Bitcoin with technical analysis: A not-so-random forest? (Gradojevic, Kukolj, Adcock & Djakovic, International Journal of Forecasting 39(1):1-17)
papers.asset_and_horizon: Bitcoin returns at hourly and daily frequency, 2015-2019.
papers.method_and_features: Random forest and other nonlinear models on popular technical indicators (trend, momentum, volume, sentiment).
papers.out_of_sample_design: Expanding-window OOS against a random walk, per the Baquero (2026) survey and the abstract. Full text was paywalled and not read, so split details are unverified.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Exact accuracies not verified (full text not accessible). Per the abstract and Baquero's survey: at hourly frequency no model significantly beats the random walk ('weakly efficient at the hourly frequency'). At daily frequency, random forest with technical indicators beats the random walk significantly.
papers.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed in a top forecasting journal with expanding-window OOS and a random-walk benchmark. Rated medium only because I could not read the full text, and the data ends in 2019.

papers.title: Bitcoin Price Prediction: Peer-Reviewed Evidence and Social Media Discourse (Baquero) - survey
papers.asset_and_horizon: Survey of 23 Bitcoin prediction studies, horizons from hourly to monthly.
papers.method_and_features: Sorts studies into tiers by evaluation method (walk-forward with naive baseline / single split / in-sample) and summarizes validated vs failed claims.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Not applicable (survey). Proposes minimum standards: walk-forward, multi-regime holdouts, naive baselines, Diebold-Mariano / model confidence sets, cost-based economic tests, preprocessing stats from the train window only.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: Secondary citations: McNally et al. 2018 daily LSTM 52% on a single split. Arain & Snudden 2025 daily OOS directional accuracy 'low-to-mid 50s', peaking around 57%, mostly near 50%. Gradojevic 2023: no model beats the random walk at hourly. Conclusion: 'Daily predictability is real but does not extend to hourly or monthly horizons, and may not survive transaction costs.'
papers.costs_considered: Summarizes Arain & Snudden (2025): statistically significant daily gains mostly fail to produce trading profits.
papers.credibility_reason: Useful map of which studies are rigorous. Single-author preprint with a small, partly hand-picked study set, and the social-media part is anecdotal.

papers.title: Bitcoin Price Direction Prediction via Regime-Aware Multi-Modal Fusion of Social Sentiment and Technical Features (Haroon)
papers.asset_and_horizon: BTC-USD hourly from yfinance, direction 3h and 6h ahead (overlapping labels).
papers.method_and_features: BiLSTM on 24 hourly OHLCV features plus Reddit FinBERT sentiment, fused by a gate driven by a volatility regime flag. Baselines: price-only BiLSTM, sentiment-only network, simple concatenation.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Single chronological split: train July 2024-June 2025 (2,146 rows), test July-Sep 2025 (1,345 rows). The regime threshold is the median volatility over the full dataset including test (look-ahead). Fixed 30 epochs with no validation set, no significance tests, one short test window.
papers.reported_direction_accuracy: 3h: price-only BiLSTM accuracy 48.83%, AUC 0.4968; proposed model accuracy 51.17%, AUC 0.5084. 6h: proposed model accuracy 48.37%, AUC 0.4902; static concatenation accuracy 52.84%, AUC 0.5253. Sentiment-only model reached F1 0.6579 by predicting 'up' 91% of the time, with AUC 0.4938.
papers.credibility_reason: Small single split, look-ahead in the regime feature, F1-led claims from near-degenerate classifiers, no costs or tests. Its one useful takeaway is the null: hourly OHLCV-only deep models scored at chance.

papers.title: Technical Analysis Meets Machine Learning: Bitcoin Evidence (Islas Anguiano & García-Medina)
papers.asset_and_horizon: BTC daily direction (not intraday), Binance data.
papers.method_and_features: LightGBM and LSTM on 95 days of binary up/down history; EMA-crossover and MACD+ADX strategies optimized on training data.
papers.out_of_sample_design: Single split: train 2021-01 to 2024-01-09 (last 20% used for validation), test 2024-01-10 to 2024-12-31, returns counted from 2024-04-14. One bull-market year (~260 test days), no walk-forward, no significance tests.
papers.costs_considered: Crudely: 0.1% per trade subtracted linearly. LSTM 53.23% (120 trades) vs buy-and-hold 42.31%; LightGBM 39.78% (136 trades), which underperformed buy-and-hold after fees.
papers.credibility_reason: Daily horizon, one test year in a strong uptrend, about 260 test points (95% CI roughly ±6pp), no baselines beyond buy-and-hold, linear cost subtraction. Included only because it is the LightGBM-on-Bitcoin paper the searches surfaced; it doesn't bear on hourly predictability.

result.consensus:
Bottom line: the credible evidence says the next hour's BTC direction is only barely predictable out of sample, and the skill is too small to survive normal trading costs. Complex models (gradient boosting, LSTMs, transformers, foundation models) don't reliably beat simple baselines at this horizon.

1) The one robust signal is short-horizon sign mean reversion (bet against the previous bar, more so after big or taker-driven moves). It was strongest at 15m: BTC AUC 0.533, 52.3% accuracy, and it held up in a frozen 2026 holdout. It fades to about AUC 0.52 at 1h (focal-coin mean) and is gone by 4h (Kitron & Wengrowicz 2026). On BTC 1h, a 3-parameter logit on lagged returns was the only model with log-loss better than the base rate. Gradient-boosted trees, an MLP and an unconstrained logit on the same inputs all did worse than just predicting the base rate.

2) Peer-reviewed hourly studies mostly find no beat of the random walk (Gradojevic et al. 2023, per abstract and survey). The most-cited positive, about 55-56% at 60 minutes (Jaquart et al. 2021), comes from one 3-month 2019 test with overlapping labels and turned negative after 30 bp costs.

3) Walk-forward, cost-aware tests on hourly BTC/USDT show naive sign-trading with XGBoost, LSTM or iTransformer collapses at 10 bp (e.g. XGBoost long-only −64% a year). Cost-filtered versions don't significantly beat buy-and-hold (Bysik & Ślepaczuk 2026).

4) Where accuracy reaches about 57%, the target is microscopic: the 10-second return after each quarter-hour, worth 0.4-0.5 bp gross (Kim & Hansen 2026).

5) Foundation models like Kronos report only small pooled crypto ICs (return IC about 0.037, below DLinear at 0.045), no direction accuracy, and no crypto trading test. Your 49-50% over 500 hours fits this. It is also too small a sample to rule out 52-53%: the 95% interval is about ±4.4 points. Telling 52% from 50% needs roughly 3,000-4,000 independent hours; your 2023-2026 data has about 25,000.

6) Polymarket changes the cost math, which matters here. Break-even as a taker at 50¢ is 51.75% (0.5 + 0.07·0.25). A binary bet pays on hit rate, not move size, so a 52-53% hit rate that is worthless in basis points could in principle clear the taker fee. By my own rough conversion (not a figure from any paper), AUC 0.52 is about 51.5% accuracy, which sits at or below the taker break-even. As a zero-fee maker it would be slightly positive, before the risk that fills come mostly when you're wrong.

7) The real benchmark is the Polymarket price, not 50%. The only direct Polymarket study (OpenMarket, BTC 15-minute markets) found a walk-forward model with 43 Binance microstructure features slightly underperformed the market's own mid price (AUC 0.838 vs 0.841), and simulated trading lost money after fees and slippage. If the Up price at the start of the hour already reflects last hour's move, the reversal edge is gone.

Net: no credible published evidence shows technical, Qlib-style, gradient-boosting or deep-learning direction models beating the hourly BTC up/down market after costs. The best-supported uses are a very simple prior-bar reversal prior, tested against the market price, and volatility forecasts for choosing which bets to take and how big.
features_with_best_evidence: Sign of the previous bar's return, weighted by its size (bet against it). Strongest OOS evidence: BTC 15m AUC 0.533; about 0.52 at 1h (focal-coin mean); gone by 4h. Betting against the last bar captures most of the effect, and the kernel stops improving after about 3 lags. A 3-parameter constrained logit beat GBM and MLP on BTC 1h log-loss (Kitron & Wengrowicz 2026).

Size of the previous move: the chance the sign flips rises steadily with |r_{t-1}|, from 50.2% to 53.0% across deciles at 15m for crypto (same paper). Keep this as a conditioning variable rather than using raw lag-1 autocorrelation, which is near zero for BTC.

Taker-flow direction of the prior bar (taker-buy vs taker-sell volume from Binance klines): reversal concentrates after moves pushed by aggressive flow and grows with its intensity. Flow lags alone scored lower (AUC 0.521 vs 0.529 for signs) and added nothing once signs were included, so use it only to condition the sign signal.

The Polymarket order-book mid price at decision time: the hardest baseline to beat. A 43-feature walk-forward model couldn't beat it in BTC 15-minute markets (OpenMarket 2026). Model the gap between your probability and this price, not the gap from 50%.

Forecast size or expected volatility (e.g. Kronos forecast spread, recent realized vol) as a filter for which hours to bet and how much, not as a direction signal. Cost-aware magnitude filters were what turned hourly ML forecasts from large losses into net-positive results (Bysik & Ślepaczuk 2026). Kronos also reports gains in volatility forecasting.

Technical indicators: small additions at best. 28 indicators added significant but tiny OOS content to quarter-hour opening-return forecasts (Kim & Hansen 2026). Indicators helped 'in selected configurations' for hourly XGBoost, while EGARCH volatility features were not robust (Bysik & Ślepaczuk 2026). At hourly frequency, random forest on indicators did not beat the random walk (Gradojevic et al. 2023, per abstract).

Clock-time microstructure (weak and sub-hour): order imbalance at quarter-hour openings predicts 4-12h returns in full-sample HAC regressions, but the top-of-hour increment was insignificant (Kim & Hansen 2026). A published turn-of-the-candle effect (positive returns concentrated at minutes 0/15/30/45) and intraday time-series momentum (first half-hour predicting last half-hour; Shen, Urquhart & Wang 2022) were checked at abstract level only, not tested for hourly direction.
red_flags_common_in_this_literature: Random or shuffled train/test splits, or a single short chronological test window in one regime, often a bull year like 2024, where 'predict up' or buy-and-hold looks skilful.
Test sets too small for binary accuracy: 500 hours gives about ±4.4pp at 95% confidence, and 1,345 rows about ±2.7pp, yet papers claim 1-3pp improvements.
Overlapping labels (e.g. 60-minute direction predicted every minute) with binomial significance tests that assume independence; Jaquart et al. report p-values like 1E-297.

Look-ahead in preprocessing: normalization or regime thresholds computed on the full dataset including test (e.g. median-volatility regime flag in Haroon 2026), label horizons not purged at split boundaries, entries filled at the same close that produced the signal (flagged in the Jadouli 2026 audit).
Outright training on test data: Crone et al. (arXiv 2110.14936) found Mudassir et al.'s headline 60% direction accuracy fell to 54% once the leak was fixed.

Heavy hyperparameter and threshold search with reused validation data: thousands of entry/exit threshold combinations, tuning on one window then reusing it, 946+ candidates before a 'prospective' test. Few papers report how many configurations were tried or apply a multiple-testing correction.
No naive baseline: missing random-walk sign, prior-bar reversal, base-rate log-loss, buy-and-hold, and, for prediction markets, the market's own implied probability.

Leading with F1, recall, precision or price-level MAPE/RMSE instead of AUC or log-loss against the base rate. Degenerate always-up classifiers post high F1 with AUC below 0.5, and 95-99% 'accuracy' claims usually come from price-level error, not direction.
Class-balance artifacts: flat bars labelled 'down', labels defined relative to a training median, or up/down base rates away from 50% making raw accuracy misleading.
No transaction costs, or fees subtracted linearly after the fact. Hourly sign-rule strategies make thousands of trades and fail at 10-30 bp even when gross equity curves look strong.
Annualizing short test windows (single-quarter annualized returns of 3,000%+) and aggregate results driven by a few folds or months.

Foundation-model evaluations that pool IC across assets and frequencies, give no single-asset timing or direction accuracy, include no crypto trading test, and risk overlap between pretraining data and test periods.
Survivorship and look-ahead in universe selection, e.g. ranking coins by volume measured after the sample ends.
For binary markets specifically: judging accuracy against 50% instead of against the market price plus fee, and ignoring that maker fills are adversely selected.

result.alpha158_default_windows: Rolling windows default to [5, 10, 20, 30, 60] bars (loader.py L139: config["rolling"].get("windows", [5, 10, 20, 30, 60])). The Alpha158 handler passes "rolling": {} (handler.py L141-149), so all 29 rolling operators run over those five windows, and "exclude" defaults to [] (L141). The price block uses windows [0] only, for OPEN, HIGH, LOW and VWAP (handler.py L143-146), so it adds 4 features. The 9 KBAR features have no window. There is no "volume" block by default; if enabled, its default windows are range(5) (L134-137). Windows count rows, not time. On 1h bars, 60 means 60 hours (2.5 days), not 60 trading days. Load order: 9 kbar, then 4 price, then the rolling block grouped by operator (ROC5..ROC60, MA5..MA60, ...). All paths are in microsoft/qlib at main commit 79633dd9506e (2026-07-23).
result.alpha360_summary: Alpha360DL.get_feature_config (qlib/contrib/data/loader.py L15-58) is raw price and volume history, 6 fields x 60 lags = 360 columns. Order: CLOSE59..CLOSE1, CLOSE0, then OPEN59..0, HIGH59..0, LOW59..0, VWAP59..0, VOLUME59..0. Within each block, oldest comes first. Exact templates: "Ref($close, %d)/$close" for i in 59..1 plus "$close/$close" (L27-31); "Ref($open, %d)/$close" plus "$open/$close" (L32-36); "Ref($high, %d)/$close" (L37-41); "Ref($low, %d)/$close" (L42-46); "Ref($vwap, %d)/$close" (L47-51); "Ref($volume, %d)/($volume+1e-12)" plus "$volume/($volume+1e-12)" (L52-56). All prices are divided by the latest close and volumes by the latest volume, so CLOSE0 = VOLUME0 = 1 (comment L17-23). Handler Alpha360 (handler.py L48-90): instruments csi500 and freq day by default. Default infer_processors = [ProcessInf, ZScoreNorm(fit_start_time, fit_end_time), Fillna(0)] (L41-45). Default learn_processors = [DropnaLabel, CSZScoreNorm(label)] (L37-40). Label is "Ref($close, -2)/Ref($close, -1) - 1" (L89-90); Alpha360vwap uses "Ref($vwap, -2)/Ref($vwap, -1) - 1" (L93-95). Benchmark YAMLs override the processors to RobustZScoreNorm(fields_group=feature, clip_outlier=true) + Fillna for features and DropnaLabel + CSRankNorm(label) for labels (e.g. GRU/workflow_config_gru_Alpha360.yaml L12-25). Sequence models rebuild the tensor as x.reshape(N, 6, 60).permute(0, 2, 1) -> [N, 60 steps, 6 features] (pytorch_gru.py L336-337), so column order matters. CSI300 results: RNN-type models do best on Alpha360 (GRU IC 0.0493, ALSTM 0.0497, HIST 0.0522; README L61-70), while Linear/MLP/Transformer/TabNet do worse on it than on Alpha158. For BTC 1h, 60 lags is 60 hours. Divide-by-latest-volume features carry strong hour-of-day volume seasonality.
result.default_label: The default label for Alpha158 and Alpha360 is "Ref($close, -2)/Ref($close, -1) - 1", named LABEL0 (qlib/contrib/data/handler.py L89-90 and L151-152). The vwap variants use "Ref($vwap, -2)/Ref($vwap, -1) - 1" (L93-95, L155-157). Ref with a negative N is a forward shift (ops.py L789, L808). At row t, features use bar t's close, and the label is the return from close t+1 to close t+2. So it predicts the next bar's return after a one-bar execution lag: the signal is formed after close t and the trade happens at close t+1 (backtest deal_price: close, e.g. LightGBM/workflow_config_lightgbm_Alpha158.yaml L27). Benchmark YAMLs restate it as "Ref($close, -2) / Ref($close, -1) - 1" (GRU/workflow_config_gru_Alpha158.yaml L32). Other variants: the rolling module overrides it to "Ref($close, -{}) / Ref($close, -1) - 1".format(horizon + 1) with horizon=20 by default (qlib/contrib/rolling/base.py L57, L168-170), and benchmarks_dynamic uses horizon 20 (README L23). TCTS trains on three labels, Ref(-2)/Ref(-1)-1, Ref(-3)/Ref(-1)-1 and Ref(-4)/Ref(-1)-1 (TCTS/workflow_config_tcts_Alpha360.yaml L25-27). The high-frequency example uses the same expression on 1-minute bars (examples/highfreq/workflow_config_High_Freq_Tree_Alpha158.yaml L31). For the Polymarket hourly market decided at H:00 with bars up to H-1, the lag-free target is sign(close_H - open_H), i.e. at row H-1: (Ref($close,-1) - Ref($open,-1)) > 0, or roughly Ref($close,-1)/$close - 1. Using Qlib's default label unchanged would train on hour H+1, which is off by one bar.
result.default_processors:
Code defaults (qlib/contrib/data/handler.py):
- _DEFAULT_LEARN_PROCESSORS = [DropnaLabel, CSZScoreNorm(fields_group="label")] (L37-40).
- _DEFAULT_INFER_PROCESSORS = [ProcessInf, ZScoreNorm, Fillna] (L41-45).
- Alpha360 uses both lists (L55-56).
- Alpha158 uses infer_processors=[] (no feature normalization) and the default learn processors, with process_type PTYPE_A ("append": learn data = infer processors then learn processors; handler.py L425-430 in qlib/data/dataset/handler.py) (L105-109).
- fit_start_time/fit_end_time are injected into any processor whose signature has them (check_transform_proc L12-34).

Benchmark overrides:
- LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost/DoubleEnsemble keep the defaults.
- Linear, GRU, LSTM, ALSTM, Transformer, TRA, TCTS and others use infer [RobustZScoreNorm(feature, clip_outlier=true), Fillna(feature)] and learn [DropnaLabel, CSRankNorm(label)] (Linear/workflow_config_linear_Alpha158.yaml L12-24).
- The 20-feature models first apply FilterCol with ["RESI5","WVMA5","RSQR5","KLEN","RSQR10","CORR5","CORD5","CORR10","ROC60","RESI10","VSTD5","RSQR60","CORR60","WVMA60","STD5","RSQR20","CORD60","CORD10","CORR20","KLOW"] (GRU/workflow_config_gru_Alpha158.yaml L13-19).
- MLP Alpha158 uses infer [DropCol VWAP0, CSZFillna] and learn [DropCol VWAP0, DropnaProcessor(feature), DropnaLabel, CSZScoreNorm(label)] with process_type independent (MLP yaml L12-37).

Implementations (qlib/data/dataset/processor.py). These are time-series (pooled over the fit window) and valid for one asset:
- ZScoreNorm L228-259: nanmean/nanstd over fit window rows; columns with std 0 are left unchanged.
- RobustZScoreNorm L262-297: median, then MAD*1.4826 (+EPS), then clip to [-3, 3].
- MinMaxNorm L196-225.
- Fillna L179-193: fill with 0.
- DropnaLabel L105-111: not used at inference.
- DropCol / FilterCol L114-143.
- TanhProcess L146-158.

These are cross-sectional (group by datetime) and meaningless for a single asset:
- CSZScoreNorm L300-323 uses zscore = (x - x.mean()).div(x.std()) (qlib/utils/data.py L35-36). With one row per timestamp, std (ddof=1) is NaN, so every label becomes NaN.
- CSRankNorm L326-359 computes rank(pct) per datetime, subtracts 0.5 and multiplies by 3.46. With one row, every label becomes the constant 1.73.
- CSZFillna L362-371 fills with the cross-sectional mean, so NaNs stay NaN.
- ProcessInf L161-176 replaces inf with the mean of non-inf values per datetime group, so for one asset inf becomes NaN (then Fillna makes it 0).
- robust_zscore for CSZScoreNorm(method="robust") (utils/data.py L16-32).

For BTC: replace label normalization with none (or a train-window z-score, or a binary sign target), and keep RobustZScoreNorm or ZScoreNorm refit on each training window.
result.operator_semantics:
Source: qlib/data/ops.py, Cython helpers in qlib/data/_libs/rolling.pyx, commit 79633dd.

General rules:
- Every operator works on one instrument's time series indexed by calendar row. Nothing in ops.py is cross-sectional, and windows count rows (bars), not clock time.
- Expression strings are parsed by parse_field (qlib/utils/__init__.py L277-302): "$x" becomes Feature("x"), "Op(" becomes Operators.Op(, then Python eval runs, so normal Python precedence applies.
- + - * / map to Add/Sub/Mul/Div (np.add/subtract/multiply/divide). x/0 gives ±inf, not NaN.
- > < >= <= == != map to Gt/Lt/Ge/Le/Eq/Ne (np.greater etc.) and return booleans; NaN compares False (base.py L32-110).
- At load time the query start moves back by get_extended_window_size (Rolling: N-1; Ref: N; data.py L852-854), so the requested range has full windows if history exists. Results are then cast to float32 (data.py L872).

Operators:
- Ref(x, N) (L781-809): series.shift(N). N>0 means N bars ago, N<0 means future (used for labels). N==0 returns the FIRST value of the loaded series, not the current one.
- Rolling base (L742-755): int N>0 uses series.rolling(N, min_periods=1).<func>(); N==0 uses expanding(min_periods=1); a float 0<N<1 uses ewm(alpha=N, min_periods=1).mean(). Windows trail and include the current bar t (right-aligned). With min_periods=1, windows are partial at the start of history and NaNs inside a window are skipped, not propagated.
- Mean (L827) and Sum (L847): pandas rolling mean and sum.
- Std (L867): pandas rolling std with ddof=1, so NaN when only 1 valid value. Var (L887) likewise.
- Max (L951) and Min (L999): rolling max and min.
- Quantile(x, N, q) (L1047-1076): rolling(N, min_periods=1).quantile(q), linear interpolation.
- Rank(x, N) (L1133-1168): rank over TIME. rolling(N, min_periods=1).rank(pct=True) with pandas>=1.4 (average ties, ascending), giving the percentile of the current value among the last N values of the same series, in (0, 1]. On older pandas it falls back to scipy percentileofscore(x1, x1[-1])/100. It is not cross-sectional; only the CSRankNorm processor is.
- IdxMax(x, N) (L971-996) and IdxMin (L1019-1044): rolling(N, min_periods=1).apply(lambda x: x.argmax()+1, raw=True), i.e. the 1-based position of the max/min inside the window counted from the OLDEST bar (N = current bar). The first occurrence wins ties, and a NaN inside the window wins argmax/argmin.
- Slope(x, N) (L1221-1254; rolling.pyx L49-88): OLS slope of y on positions 1..N (oldest=1, current=N), using only non-NaN points: (n*Sxy - Sx*Sy)/(n*Sxx - Sx^2), n = number of non-NaN points. 0/0 gives NaN when n=1.
- Rsquare(x, N) (L1257-1283; rolling.pyx L137-182): squared Pearson r between y and positions 1..N. Set to NaN where rolling(N, min_periods=1).std() of x is close to 0 with atol=2e-5 (L1282).
- Resi(x, N) (L1286-1311; rolling.pyx L91-134): residual of the CURRENT bar against that window's OLS line: y_t - (slope*N + (ybar - slope*xbar)).
- Corr(a, b, N) (L1467-1498): pandas a.rolling(N, min_periods=1).corr(b) (Pearson). Set to NaN where the rolling std of a or of b is close to 0 (atol=2e-5, L1494-1497). Cov (L1501) is the rolling cov.
- Log (L167-182) is np.log with no guard. Abs is np.abs. Sign casts to float32, then np.sign.
- Greater(a, b) (L438-455) is np.maximum and Less (L458-475) is np.minimum. These are element-wise max/min of two series or a series and a scalar, NaN-propagating, not comparisons.
- Delta(x, N) = x - x.shift(N).
- Mad, Med, Skew (N>=3), Kurt (N>=4), Count, WMA and EMA also exist but Alpha158/Alpha360 do not use them.

Exact-reproduction details: Qlib stores bins as float32. Rolling ops on bool series (e.g. $close>Ref($close,1)) are averaged as 0/1.

A router (RNN over each sample's history of per-predictor losses plus latent state) picks a predictor with gumbel-softmax. Training assigns samples to predictors via optimal transport over daily batches (MTSDatasetH, use_daily_transport). A regime-switching idea that suits drift. For one asset, define batches over time windows instead of days. Imports matplotlib/tqdm/tensorboard only for logging.

models.name: TFT (examples/benchmarks/TFT/tft.py)

models.name: ADD (pytorch_add.py)
models.notes: Adversarial split into 'excess' and 'market' parts with a gradient-reversal layer. The market label is the cross-sectional mean return per datetime cut into tertiles (gen_market_label L351-361), which is undefined for a lone asset (excess = 0). For BTC it would need a substitute regime label, e.g. volatility tertile.

models.name: AdaRNN (pytorch_adarnn.py)
models.notes: Built for concept drift: splits the training period into maximally dissimilar periods and adds a distribution-matching loss (MMD/cosine/adversarial, TransferLoss L554) on the RNN hidden states with learned per-step weights. Works per series, so it fits single-asset hourly data.

models.name: TCTS (pytorch_tcts.py)
models.notes: A GRU forecaster with 3 outputs (horizons t+2, t+3, t+4, yaml L25-27, output_dim 3). A weight network sets per-sample, per-task loss weights using (feature, error, label, init_pred, task embedding) and is trained on the validation loss of target_label 0 (train_epoch L134-200). For BTC, use auxiliary horizons such as 2h and 4h returns, or |return|.

models.name: IGMTF (pytorch_igmtf.py)
models.notes: Per day: mean hidden state of the stocks gives a day vector, which finds the k_day=10 most similar training days; then n_neighbor=10 nearest training samples by cosine similarity are aggregated (forward L404-442). With one asset, the day vector is one sample, so it turns into nearest-neighbour analog retrieval over past hours. Uses a pretrained LSTM (yaml model_path).

DDG-DA[LightGBM] IC 0.0878, ICIR 0.6185, Ann 0.1261, IR 2.0096, MDD -0.0744.
models.notes: These are training schemes, not predictors. The higher ICs reflect a 20-day label horizon, so they are not comparable to the 1-day tables. With a linear base (the default for the DDG-DA example), the meta model is torch: a closed-form weighted ridge theta = (X^T W X + alpha I)^-1 X^T W y (net.py L65-70), with period weights from a linear layer over hist_step_n=30 periods of proxy-model performance (TimeWeightMeta L11-40). The proxy performance and the default ic_loss are cross-sectional Spearman/IC per date, so for one asset switch to criterion 'mse' (model.py L93-104).

result.rolling_retraining:
1) RollingGen (qlib/workflow/task/gen.py L140-300) turns one task into a sequence of tasks.
- step: default 40 calendar steps (L146).
- rtype: ROLL_EX (default) keeps the start date and expands the train segment; ROLL_SD slides fixed-size segments. Valid and test always slide (L141-142, L207-215).
- The first test segment is [test_start, test_start+step-1] (L289-290). Each next task shifts by step until test_end (gen_following_tasks L187-226).
- trunc_segments (L126-137) cuts the end of train/valid by trunc_days before test start, to avoid label leakage.
- handler_mod (L94-123) extends the handler end_time.
- MultiHorizonGenBase (L304-347) clones a task per horizon and truncates by horizon + label_leak_n (2).

2) Offline rolling driver: qlib/contrib/rolling/base.py class Rolling (L24).
- Defaults horizon=20 and step=20 (L57-58).
- Rewrites the label to "Ref($close, -{}) / Ref($close, -1) - 1".format(horizon + 1) (L168-170).
- Builds tasks with RollingGen(step=self.step, trunc_days=self.horizon + 1) (L197-199).
- Trains each task with TrainerR, then concatenates each window's out-of-sample predictions (_ens_rolling L218-229).
- Example: examples/benchmarks_dynamic/baseline/rolling_benchmark.py (horizon=20, L22). Run with python -m qlib.contrib.rolling.base --conf_path <yaml> run.

3) DDG-DA, for concept drift: qlib/contrib/rolling/ddgda.py class DDGDA(Rolling) (L70-127).
- Params: sim_task_model 'gbdt' (proxy), alpha 0.01 (ridge L2), loss_skip_thresh 50, fea_imp_n 30, segments 0.62, hist_step_n 30.
- Step 1: train a proxy model per rolling period and build a matrix of each period's model tested on every day. The metric is per-datetime Spearman IC (meta/data_selection/dataset.py _calc_perf L107-111).
- Step 2: a meta model learns sample weights per past period from the last hist_step_n rows of that matrix (net.py TimeWeightMeta L11-40: Linear(hist_step_n, 1), centered and scaled by k, exp/clamp or tanh).
- The weights are trained so that a closed-form weighted ridge fit on reweighted history does best on the next period (PredNet.forward L65-70). Criterion: ICLoss (utils.py L12-64; skips dates with fewer than skip_size samples, L40) or MSE (model.py L93-104).
- The learned weights then feed a Reweighter into the real model's rolling fits.
- Example: examples/benchmarks_dynamic/DDG-DA/workflow.py (linear by default, L24).

4) Online serving: qlib/workflow/online/strategy.py RollingStrategy (L92) with prepare_tasks(cur_time) (L167) creates new RollingGen tasks as the calendar advances. Examples: examples/online_srv/rolling_online_management.py and online_management_simulate.py; examples/model_rolling/task_manager_rolling.py.

5) examples/rolling_process_data refits learnable processors (ZScore mean/std etc.) inside each rolling window instead of once (README).

6) Drift-aware models: AdaRNN (distribution matching across periods), TRA (router over latent regimes), TCTS (auxiliary-task scheduling), DoubleEnsemble (sample reweighting and feature selection).

For BTC 1h: implement walk-forward yourself (e.g. expanding or sliding train window, retrain every 168-720 bars). Leave a gap of at least the label look-ahead (1 bar for a same-hour target, 2 for Qlib's default label) between train end and test start. Refit normalizers per window. Use MSE or log-loss, not IC, as the DDG-DA criterion.

- 1-minute OHLC plus Simpson VWAP "($open + 2*$high + 2*$low + $close)/6" (L46), normalized by the previous day's last close, "Cut({0}/Ref(DayLast({1}), 240), 240, None)" (L51-53).

3) qlib/contrib/data/highfreq_handler.py (HighFreqHandler, HighFreqGeneralHandler with day_length, HighFreqOrderHandler, backtest handlers) plus highfreq_processor.py and highfreq_provider.py are feature pipelines for RL order execution (examples/rl_order_execution). They have no prediction labels and target execution, not direction.

Nothing in Qlib targets hourly bars or a single-instrument directional forecast. The pieces carry over only as an expression engine plus the generic models.
caveats_for_single_asset_hourly: Label off-by-one: Qlib's default label Ref($close,-2)/Ref($close,-1)-1 skips a bar (signal after close t, trade at close t+1). For a bet placed at H:00 on hour H, the target is sign(close_H - open_H), i.e. (Ref($close,-1)-Ref($open,-1))>0 at row H-1. The default would silently train on hour H+1.

Cross-sectional label processors break. CSZScoreNorm computes (x-mean)/std per datetime; with 1 row std is NaN, so every label is NaN. CSRankNorm gives the constant (1-0.5)*3.46 = 1.73. CSZFillna does nothing. ProcessInf turns inf into NaN. Replace them with a train-window z-score, raw returns, or a binary sign target.

Every benchmark IC, ICIR and Rank IC is a per-date cross-sectional correlation across about 300 CSI300 stocks (qlib/contrib/eva/alpha.py calc_ic L177-179), averaged over days. With one asset per timestamp it is undefined. Use hit rate, log loss/Brier, calibration, time-series correlation over rolling windows, and PnL net of the 0.07*p*(1-p) taker fee.

Benchmark numbers do not transfer. They are daily China A-shares, CSI300 2017-01..2020-08, long-only TopkDropout (top 50, drop 5) excess return vs SH000300, with 5bp/15bp costs and a 9.5% limit move. A cross-sectional IC of about 0.04-0.05 comes from ranking many stocks, not predicting one direction. The only intraday benchmark (1-min, CSI300) reached about 51.1% long precision even when picking the top 20% of stocks each minute. BTC as a taker needs about 51.75% with no selection.

Model families that depend on the cross-section collapse or need redesign for one asset: GATs (attention over same-day stocks), HIST (stock-concept matrix), ADD (market label = cross-sectional mean return), IGMTF (day vector = mean over stocks), TRA (daily optimal transport batches), HFLGBModel (demeaned labels become all 0, so all class 1), and DDG-DA (per-date Spearman proxy performance and ICLoss that skips dates with fewer than 50 samples).

Window scale: Alpha158 windows [5,10,20,30,60] and Alpha360's 60 lags cover at most 60 hours. They miss the daily and weekly cycles that dominate BTC hourly volatility and volume. Consider added windows such as 24/72/168/336/720 bars, or at least test the rescaling.

Intraday seasonality: nothing in Alpha158/360 encodes hour-of-day or day-of-week. Volume-ratio features (VMA, VSTD, VSUMP, VOLUME{i}) are dominated by hour-of-day volume patterns (US/EU sessions, funding at 00/08/16 UTC). Add calendar features or deseasonalize volume, e.g. divide by the trailing same-hour median.

Calendar gaps: Qlib windows count rows. Reindex Binance 1h klines to a complete UTC hourly calendar with NaN for missing hours (exchange maintenance), or Ref and rolling windows will silently span gaps. Remember min_periods=1 lets partial windows through at the start of history; drop the first 60+ bars.

Timing and look-ahead: features at row H-1 use the H-1 close, which is only final at H:00:00. The decision at the hour open must use the closed candle (poll after close, and allow for API latency). Fit normalizers only on the training window; Qlib's comments warn fit_end_time must not include test data (processor.py L198-199, L232-233).

No $vwap in Binance klines: compute it as quote_volume/volume. Qlib's Yahoo data without VWAP had those factors zero-filled, which made DDG-DA's regression rank-deficient (benchmarks_dynamic README L26). Crypto has no split/dividend factor, no suspended days and no limit moves, so CN-data adjustments and filters (limit_threshold, $factor, paused) do not apply.

Sample size: 2023-10-19..2026-09-13 is about 1,060 days, roughly 25,400 hourly rows for one series, with heavily overlapping rolling features. CSI300 training (2008-2014) is about 1,700 days x 300 stocks, roughly 500k rows. Deep models (Transformer, TabNet, TRA, GRU on 158 features) will overfit. Prefer ridge/logistic or a small MLP with strong regularization, purged walk-forward validation, and a gap of at least the label look-ahead (Qlib's rolling uses trunc_days = horizon+1).

Size vs direction: the LightGBM top-20 feature list used by GRU/LSTM/ALSTM/GATs/TRA/TFT (RESI5, WVMA5, RSQR5, KLEN, RSQR10, CORR5, CORD5, CORR10, ROC60, RESI10, VSTD5, RSQR60, CORR60, WVMA60, STD5, RSQR20, CORD60, CORD10, CORR20, KLOW) is mostly volatility and shape features. Expect them to forecast |return| (like the Kronos spread), not its sign. A size forecast alone gives no Up/Down edge; it only sharpens a probability if some drift estimate exists (P(up) ~ Phi(mu/sigma)).

Loss choice: Qlib trains MSE on continuous returns, so a few large-move hours dominate the fit. The Polymarket payoff is binary, so train on the sign with BCE/log loss, or evaluate calibrated P(up) against the market price. The trading edge is P(up) minus the Polymarket price, not the return forecast.
Metric scaling: SigAnaRecord and risk analysis annualize with ann_scaler 252 (e.g. LightGBM yaml L67). Hourly 24/7 data needs 8760.

Feature quirks to reproduce or fix on purpose: ROC{d} is Ref(close,d)/close, the inverse of momentum. STD{d} is std of price levels, not returns. IMAX/IMIN are 1-based positions from the oldest bar (1.0 = current bar), and the IMXD comment's sign interpretation contradicts the code. CORD takes log(volume ratio + 1). Corr and Rsquare become NaN when a rolling std is under an absolute tolerance of 2e-5, which matters if applied to normalized inputs. Qlib stores and casts to float32 (data.py L872).

Non-stationarity: BTC volatility and volume regimes shift a lot from 2023 to 2026. A single fixed fit window for RobustZScoreNorm/ZScoreNorm, as in the benchmark YAMLs, will drift. Refit per rolling window (examples/rolling_process_data), or use rolling-window normalization inside the features.

Benchmark README hygiene: CSI500 DoubleEnsemble rows repeat Linear's Ann/IR/MDD exactly (README L118, L126), and TFT's Rank IC (0.0116) is far below its IC. Treat the tables as rough, seed-averaged (20 runs) indications, not ground truth.

checks.item: Kitron & Wengrowicz (arXiv 2608.21888): existence, universe, horizons, walk-forward geometry, dates, holdout
checks.evidence: Paper exists (22 Aug 2026). 183 Binance USDT spot pairs vs 187 US stocks/ETFs; 15m primary, focal panel 5m-4h. Train 5,760/test 960 (1h: 2,160/360). Primary 2025-01-01 to 2026-02-11; frozen holdout 2026-02-12 to 2026-08-08. Design fixed before wide run (not preregistered). Label 1[close>open], flat bars = 0. Controls confirmed in App. B.4/D: exact permutation null, shuffled labels (0/370 significant), sign-randomization (0/14), one-bar gap (71% of excess survives), Coinbase/OKX/Bybit refetch. Post-sample volume ranking, flat-bar inflation and 'optimistic by a third to a half' all stated. Authors disclose they run a trading system using a variant of the model.

checks.item: Bysik & Slepaczuk (arXiv 2606.00060): data, walk-forward, trading numbers, costs, inference
checks.evidence: Binance BTC/USDT USD-margined futures, hourly, 70,872 obs. Rolling 12/3/3-month folds, 27 folds, features and scaling done inside each fold. Table 4: XGB LO gross 73.50%, 10 bp -64.00% (10,619 trades), LSTM -50.65%, iTransformer -83.93%, 24h momentum -45.93%, XGB LS -92.58%, B&H 56.35%. Table 11/18: cost-aware LO 65.40%, SR 1.09, 251 trades, 16/27 profitable folds, median fold ARC 7.98%, median 4 trades per fold. Table 8: dSR vs B&H 0.27, CI [-0.46, 0.95], not significant. Circular block bootstrap 24/72/168h with Holm; cost grid 0-25 bp; no depth, partial fills or maker/taker routing. Hit rate only called 'positive but moderate'; no numeric accuracy found.
checks.correction: The out-of-sample test period is 2019-04-01 to 2025-12-31 (Table D.31, fold 1 starts 2019-04-01), not 2018-2025. The '94 candidates, 3-336h windows, Spearman' indicator detail is unverified (only the 10 TA selection groups were seen). Two selection-risk points strengthen the finding's skepticism: lambda=2.0 (the headline spec) is the single best point of the reported lambda grid, and 10 of 27 folds contain exactly 1 trade (effectively buy-and-hold).

checks.item: Consensus bottom line: next-hour direction skill 'too small to survive normal trading costs'
checks.evidence: Every cost result cited is in basis points of notional on spot or perps (Kitron 5-20 bp, Bysik 10 bp, Kim & Hansen 5 bp, Jaquart). Binary payoffs depend on hit rate, not move size, as the consensus admits in point 6. Kitron's own BTC 15m pair (AUC 0.533 <-> 52.3%) matches the binormal conversion acc = Phi(sqrt(2)*Phi^-1(AUC)/2), which also gives 52.3%.
checks.correction: For hourly the conclusion probably still holds, but for a different reason. The focal-coin 1h AUC 0.521 converts to ~51.4%; BTC is the weakest focal coin; the fit-conditional headline is optimistic by a third to a half; and the 15m holdout decayed 0.531 -> 0.522. That puts BTC 1h plausibly near 51%, below the 51.75% taker break-even. It is not shown that spot-cost evidence transfers. At 15m, BTC's 52.3% unthresholded and ~56% on the most confident few percent would sit at or above a binary break-even, so 'too small for costs' is overstated for Polymarket-style payoffs at shorter horizons.
